# []{#anchor}Study Site

Newborough Warren occupies the south-western tip of the Isle of Anglesey in north-west Wales (Figure 1). The dune field is underlain by weakly permeable glacial till forming the effective base of the sand aquifer. A bedrock ridge, demarcated by the 20 m AOD contour of the DEM and trending south-west to north-east, forms the northern boundary of the study area. To the south the ridge plunges beneath the dune field; its northern end reaches the coast, meeting the sea obliquely rather than face-on. The hydrological study area, defined by the extent of the DEM-derived flow network (modelled drainage lines from topographic analysis of the digital elevation model, not mapped surface watercourses; the network itself is not drawn), covers approximately 865 ha (\~4.3 km × 3.9 km; the hydrological study area outlined in Figure 1). The monitoring network spans \~3.0 km × 2.1 km within this, lying entirely on the south-eastern flank of the ridge. The dune system on the north-western flank of the ridge, draining toward the Malltraeth estuary, is hydrologically separate from the main Newborough Warren aquifer; monitoring wells located on that flank do not have sufficient record length for inclusion in the clustering and state-space analyses reported here.

Lateral recharge from the rock ridge into the dune sands has been identified as a possible contribution to the aquifer\'s water balance (Stratford et al., 2007). The dune aquifer south-east of the ridge is divided into an eastern block, where shallower sand over till and estuarine deposits produces a more responsive, heterogeneous water table regime, and a western block, where deep sand accumulation over a broader platform permits significant groundwater storage and more buffered seasonal fluctuations (Stratford et al., 2007).

The aquifer discharges principally across the south-western foreshore (Caernarfon Bay) and the southern and eastern coast (Menai Strait) as tides recede. A small lake within the warren, Llyn Rhos-Ddu, acts as a near-fixed head body and is the dominant local drainage sink for the immediately adjacent C1 Lake Edge wells; it receives groundwater for most of the year as the regional water table maintains its head above the lake bed, and supplements aquifer recharge during the driest months (Stratford et al., 2007). The active monitoring network comprises 89 measuring points (Figure 1). Of these, 88 are dipwells forming the analytical network used in this study --- 66 reference-network wells with sufficient record length and consistent monitoring for inclusion in the core analyses, plus 22 extended-network wells used in robustness checks and spatial interpolation. The Llyn Rhos-Ddu lake gauge is the 89th point. Ten further located points --- nine dipwells whose records are too sparse for inclusion and one with no record --- are not shown. An interactive map of the monitoring network is linked in Section 10, and the wells can also be explored in the groundwater flooding forecaster (forecaster.html).

The northern 700 hectares are managed plantation dominated by mature Corsican pine (Stratford et al., 2007). A partial clearance of approximately 4.2 ha (about 0.6% of the plantation) began in December 2017, removing trees across a defined felling zone at the plantation--open dune transition (Figure 2). Dune scraping has been undertaken at selected western slack locations: CEH36 in April 2015, and CEH18 and CEH21 in October 2023.

The dune slack communities at Newborough Warren are classified under the National Vegetation Classification as SD15b (wet slack, **Salix repens--Calliergon cuspidatum** community) and SD16 (dry slack, **Salix repens--Holcus lanatus** community). Curreli et al. (2013) (see also Davy et al., 2006) measured the water table regimes of these communities in a site-specific vegetation survey across Newborough Warren and four other Welsh dune systems: Curreli\'s wet-slack (SD15b) community mean summer minimum is 0.61 m below the ground surface, and its winter maximum floods the slack, to a community mean of 0.21 m above the surface; the dry-slack (SD16) community means are a summer minimum of 0.98 m and a winter maximum within 0.25 m of the surface. These thresholds provide the ecological reference frame for all hydrological assessments in this study. Wells whose mean summer minimum exceeds 0.98 m are classified as ecologically critical --- beyond the range of SD16 viability. For the purposes of assessing management options, two intermediate bands are defined: wells between 0.61 m and 0.75 m below ground are likely to be recoverable to SD15b viability by a standard dune scraping event yielding approximately 0.14 m of water-table benefit (a planning assumption; at CEH36 the BACI-measured benefit is +0.13 m, from a cut whose depth, inferred from that response, is about 0.43 m, consistent with field observation; Section 4.5); wells between 0.98 m and 1.20 m are likely to be recoverable to SD16 dry slack viability, 1.20 m reflecting a planning assumption of about 0.22 m of benefit from a deeper scrape rather than a benefit measured at any well. These \"recoverable\" classifications should be treated as indicative --- achievable excavation depth varies with substrate, access and licence conditions, and the empirical basis is a single scraping event at one well. Wells deeper than 1.20 m are beyond the reach of a standard single scraping event under average antecedent conditions.
